title: Zen and Creativity Class 2 Part 3
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton leads a haiku-writing session in the Zen and Creativity class, with participants working from a table of photographs, including an aspen grove, a Kansas prairie, and Castle Rock. Members read their poems aloud, such as "Pinned by the sun, timeless hours, no place better than here" and "Can you see a warm breeze? Can you hear the blue sky?" Shuko asks what lies beyond what the eye sees, and the group describes their process: one person lies back and riffs on a train whistle, another struggles to find words for the dusty smell of a summer wood. Someone says the practice feels relational, with the tree and the poet writing each other. The session closes with scheduling for the next meeting and an assignment to bring a favorite Zen saying, typed out, to share.

Oh, good.
I'm sort of determined to not look at anything else, just to see what happens.
Yeah.
See if I get bored with it, or think of things.
So, under the aspen tree, I can't see the beetles, the ants, the ones I don't know.
I'm just sort of thinking about it.
Great.
It's obvious to write about what you can see.
Yeah, great.
And then what about what you can't see that you don't even know you can see?
So, we'll go around several times.
So, John?
Okay.
I wrote about this place, and the first one I tried to mostly write about what I saw.
And I can just, boy, I can just close my eyes.
I've been to this place many times, and I can just picture it.
So, I wrote:
*Bright, still, the ocean's diamonds sparkle, sweet dusty smell, a dragonfly passes.*
Nice.
Very nice.
Very high-cool.
I was kind of inspired by several of the tree photos that are sitting around.
And by pencil and paper.
*Ancient trees and old growth forests, I offer my thanks.*
Beautiful.
*A woman sits by herself without thinking.
She remembers.*
Oh, I love that.
Which is one that I, there's a place in [unclear: "outer"].
*Fallen oak leaves warm, the moccasin soft trail, dappled August sings me up.*
Terry, I was sort of thinking about the process, you know, about writing that's going on.
I also wrote:
*The poet sits gazing, the tree moves softly in the breeze, composing its own poem.*
Who's writing?
You know, who's the poet here?
Right.
Yeah.
See, my other one, same place, I was just trying to write about what it felt like, not thinking visually.
And I wrote:
*Pinned by the sun, timeless hours, no place better than here.*
Pinned by the sun.
*The stone Buddha sits in flickering candle glow, watching as I write.*
Do you have another one with you?
I do, I have 11.
Oh gosh, this is the right group.
*A woman walks a dangerous path, carrying an empty cup, sheep scamper past.*
I actually saw a video today of the most dangerous path on earth, the scariest hike.
It's in Spain, and it was amazing to see it.

I don't know how they videoed it, but there were these incredibly high precipices, and then these amazing narrow bars that they would put in between outcroppings, and then the worn, kind of step-like, ladder-y things in these caves.
It was actually used for people to carry things that they were marketing.
So, you can hardly imagine walking that path.
It came to mind as a metaphor.
Some more?
I started thinking about senses and perceptions.
So:
*Can you see a warm breeze?
Can you hear the blue sky?
Don't be so sure.*
I only wrote two, I'm tapped out.
Any more, Terry?
Yeah, I had a couple that were inspired by the Kansas photo.
*Kansas prairie, wide blue skies reflect in still water on the Zendo floor.*
That's true.
A lot of stuff on that Zendo floor.
*Blue-green mountain water, sounds of breathing, treasures sparkle.*
So, you two just wrote, and there was no impediment.
What was your process like?
Did you notice any challenges?
I ran through different sorts of areas, I guess.
At first, I was just looking at the actual image, thinking about the colors and shapes.
Then, from there, I just started thinking about what can you not see?
Then, after a while, I forgot about all the other senses.
It was only vision.
I was thinking about hearing.
I actually didn't think about smelling at all.
Then, I laid back and I closed my eyes and heard the train whistle.
So, I ran with the train whistling.
I kept riffing on it.
I got a little bored.
There was even time for that!
What spaciousness!
How about you, John?
I was just trying to put myself there.
Just remember what I experienced, what I saw, what I felt in my body, what I heard.
I struggled finding words.
Nothing surprising.
But it was enjoyable.
It was enjoyable to try to put just a few words to that, to a place that I'd been many times, that I'd had a lot of information to sift through.
It's been interesting to hear what other people have written, what you can make out of it.
I felt like the first one was the hardest.
I had raced, I think, a few times on that.
But then, once I got the rhythm cadence in my mind, I didn't have to mess with rhythm anymore.
It's interesting.
I actually thought, as I was writing this one, that others may pick up on the same thing.
You just mentioned it.
You did.
*Loud and dissonant.
Minor brass chords.*
A jazz band?
A passing train.
You guys are good.
Any comments about your process?
Yeah, this one is probably going to say something about that.
*Walking far from civilization, I stopped beside the trail.
A crying flower.*
It seems to me that each one was like this little meditation of being in the moment.
I studied the rhythm from hearing these.
Then, I listened to what you said about the different elements of a haiku.
Then, I just wrote, kept writing them, and writing them, and writing them.
Because it was fun.
It was really fun.
Then, after all, I don't know if they're good, but each one seems meaningful.
That's the point.
Well, it's satisfying.
That sort of captures what I'm experiencing.
The more you do it, the more you can contrast the right things to get the punch.
Exactly.
The other thing I was thinking about was the way writing and perceiving and putting yourself in these different positions.
I like the way it's such a relational thing.
It's not a neutral thing.
I had a couple about the tree's relationship to the poet.
So, I read one.
Here's another one.
I did two on that.
Another one, just directly about writing:
*Something about writing.
Exciting, confusing, mysterious.
How does a tree feel about its work?*
This photo is very evocative for me because I went to the Castle Rock many times in the years that I lived in California.
In fact, my family and I found it when it was not even open as a regional park.
We were in there and we found that there were signs saying, "No trespassing and you will be shot."
Things like that.
It was really kind of scary in there because nobody knew about it.
It eventually got incorporated as a regional park.
It was so magical in there.
It was so warm in the summer.
Yet it was all shaded and so forth.
So soft.
There was a lot of sounds and smells.
I couldn't work that in, all of those things.
I could really just do mostly the visual and a little bit of the soft sound, I guess.
It was tactically so satisfying on this very soft padded trail.
I had a hard time reducing.
I could work on this a long time before it would satisfy a sensation that I wanted to.
I like your use of the word lots.
There is a great smell in the woods.
It's kind of like a dusty smell.
You can smell the trees and there's dust.
It's in the summer when you're hiking.
I love that.
I was trying to find words for that and I'd have to work on that a lot.
For one thing, these are kind of kernels of something that we can work on further.
Maybe do a series of the same picture.
I like the idea of either writing a lot about one picture or trying to make one poem say a lot about one place.
It's a different approach.
That's what skinned me with what you're saying.
You really gave us some great stuff to work on.
Yes, thank you.
Every time I'm surprised, I go, oh gosh.
It's really just somebody giving you a question to sit there and do it.
Meditation helps a lot to really observe closely.
Would you say though, I think a lot of what I was feeling onto the surface was trying to come out through the writing.
I liked what you said about Japanese style.
There's certain aspects to nature and the sentiment that's expressed in the haikus that people strive to embody in their lives.
There's a real philosophy in a sense.
I wanted to find that, but I kept experiencing myself as a 20th century kind of person instead of the ancient Japanese writer.
There was an interesting play with that.
I was really searching for the same undercurrent in me that they were searching for in the work.
I'd like to take it a step deeper to find ways to capture that essence of the stream that I was trying to swim in.
Well, for next time, Monday is the 14th, and you said you probably won't be able to come.
If you could come on the Saturday, it's fine if you want to do that.
Saturday the 20th or whatever? 19th.
I'll see when I might be able to do that.
At 9?
At 30.
Will you be able to come next week?
That's Valentine's Day.
The command performance day.
So you were saying the following?
Monday's first?
Yeah, then Saturday's second.
I don't know if we're getting, you're going to be out of town, so we won't be here at all.
Maybe we should just meet on that Saturday.
Yeah, it could be.
We could come all day on that Saturday.
Have you heard from the other people who signed up for Monday?
Yeah, I have too.
Is there an assignment for that?
Yes, yeah.
Bring a copy, a written down copy of a favorite Zen saying of yours.
Type it or something so that other people can see it, because you won't necessarily be doing something with it, although you might.
In other words, it's kind of like sharing a pool of stuff that people can use.
Okay, great.
